summary: A 1978 description of MARS, a Message Archiving and Retrieval Service developed at Computer Corporation of America using the Datacomputer, a network database utility.

plainLanguage.summary: A big shared filing cabinet for messages that you can store things in and search later. This is how one was built.

questions: how did early networks archive messages
how do you search an archived message collection
subtitle: A system for storing and searching archived network messages

tldr.problem: Groups on the ARPANET, particularly teleconferencing participants, needed a way to store and later retrieve messages with flexible search options, but the network had no common message archive service.
tldr.mechanism: MARS uses the Datacomputer, a network database system, to index and store messages. Messages are filed by sending them to a special mailbox (MARS-Filer), indexed by date, sender, recipient, subject words, and body text, and retrieved by sending query messages to MARS-Retriever.
tldr.outcome: A usable message archive that allows Boolean combinations of search criteria and integrates with standard mail tools, making it possible for groups to maintain and search historical correspondence.

today: MARS was an experimental service in the 1970s and is no longer in use. The concepts it introduced—message indexing, Boolean search, and integration with mail protocols—became standard features in email and groupware systems decades later. Today, message archiving and search are routine capabilities provided by modern email platforms.

sections.title: The MARS System
sections.content:
MARS (Message Archiving and Retrieval Service) was developed at Computer Corporation of America and uses the Datacomputer, a network database utility developed for ARPA. The service is available primarily to groups storing teleconferencing transcripts and to individual ARPANET users.

MARS messages are divided into public and private collections. Public messages, such as those from the Header-People group at MIT and MsgGroup proceedings at USC-ISI, can be retrieved by anyone. Private messages can be retrieved only by the archiver or named recipients. All messages are heavily indexed and can be retrieved by date, sender, recipients, subject keywords, or body text.
sections.plainLanguage: MARS lets a group store messages and search them later. Some messages are public (anyone can read), others are private (only the sender or named people can see them).

sections.title: How to Archive Messages
sections.content:
Messages are archived by sending them to MARS-Filer at CCA using standard mail tools like SNDMSG. MARS supports three filing modes: single-message mode (naming MARS-Filer as a recipient), forwarded-message mode (forwarding a message to the Filer), and batch mode (sending multiple messages in a single mail envelope with "batch" in the subject).

The Filer parses message headers to extract date, sender, recipients, and subject line, then indexes all text in the message body. One-character words in the subject and two-character words in the body are discarded. Hyphenated phrases are kept intact, and the system accommodates all RFC 733 message format variations.
sections.plainLanguage: You just mail the message to MARS-Filer. You can send one message, forward one with notes, or bundle many messages together. MARS automatically reads the date, from, to, and subject fields and remembers all the important words.

sections.title: How to Retrieve Messages
sections.content:
Retrieval is initiated by sending a specially formatted message to MARS-Retriever at CCA. The message body specifies search criteria: DATE, AFTER, BEFORE, FROM, TO, SUBJECT, and TEXT fields. Date fields support comparisons (before, after, since, until), and FROM field OR logic is implicit; TO, SUBJECT, and TEXT field logic uses AND unless OR is explicit.

An interactive TENEX program (RR.SAV) is available to compose retrieval requests, and copies are stored on the Datacomputer and at CCA and ISI. Retrieved messages are mailed back one at a time to the requester's mailbox.
sections.plainLanguage: You mail a message to MARS-Retriever saying what you're looking for: a date range, who it was from or to, or words in the subject or text. MARS mails back the matching messages.

sections.title: Integration with Existing Tools
sections.content:
MARS is designed to work naturally with existing ARPANET message handling tools. Users do not need to learn a special interface; they use familiar mail commands (SNDMSG, mail programs) to file and retrieve. The Filer checks for new messages every hour, and the Retriever checks every quarter-hour, operating as a background job during low-activity periods.

This integration was a key design principle: MARS did not require users to switch tools or adopt new behaviors. It simply sat on the network as another mail participant, handling archiving and retrieval as automated responses to messages.
sections.plainLanguage: You do not need to learn new commands. You just mail messages to special addresses, and MARS acts like another person who remembers everything and can find messages for you later.

references.text: Sattley, J., "MARS - A Message Archiving and Retrieval Service", RFC 744, January 1978.
